on the “better” side: it’s hard to overstate how unprecedented this flexibility is. you’re not locked into the circumstances you were born into in the same way. you can pivot careers, find niche communities, teach yourself things that used to require gatekeepers. for a lot of people, that’s not just convenient—it’s life-changing.

but your second point is the catch: when everything is editable, nothing feels binding. and humans seem to actually *need* some sense of constraint or continuity to feel grounded. identity used to be partially “assigned” (job, location, community), and now it’s more like a constant open-ended project. that sounds liberating, but it also quietly turns into: *if things aren’t working, is it my fault for not editing better?*

so instead of “i am a thing,” it becomes “i am a draft,” all the time.

and drafts are exhausting 😄

i think what’s happening is we’ve gained *technical freedom* faster than we’ve developed *psychological structures* to handle it. there’s no built-in stopping rule anymore. no obvious “this version of me is enough.” so people end up oscillating between reinvention and burnout.

my take? flexibility *is* better—but only if people deliberately introduce some “artificial fixed points.” like choosing commitments you *don’t* constantly optimize away: relationships, long-term projects, values, even just a place you decide to belong to. otherwise everything stays liquid, and it’s hard to stand on liquid.

so maybe the real skill now isn’t just “how do i change?” but “what do i choose not to change?”
